title: Chapter 1. The Cause of Virachandra's Descent
html:
The secret pact of Chaitanya and Nityananda in Nilachala; Nityananda at Panihati; the healing of Vasudha at Ambika-nagara and his marriage to her and to Jahnava; Nityananda revealed as Balarama; the move to Khardaha (pp. 15–27)

[p. 15]

1Glory, glory to Sri Krishna Chaitanya and Nityananda!
Glory to Sri Advaitachandra, the root of all bliss!

2Be merciful, all of you, and fulfil my desire:
I long to sing the virtues of Nityananda-chandra.

3My heart wishes to sing the virtues of Sri Virachandra —
as a tiny bird in its thirst longs for the whole ocean.

4Of what was left untold in the pastimes of Nityananda and Chaitanya
I wish to tell something in particular.

5I pray at the feet of all the Vaishnavas:
give me, all of you, the power to describe it.

6Once Nityananda and Gaurachandra, seated on one seat
in Nilachala, took this counsel in private:

7"Go to Gauda and become a householder1 —
then all these people will be delivered.

8I shall come again, into your house,
and you will know me by my true form and nature.

9In your house my incarnation will take place;2
distributing bhakti once more, I shall deliver the world.

10A hidden incarnation is not revealed in the shastras;
my pastimes are inconceivable, no one knows them.

11Without your mercy no one knows me:
he alone knows to whom you give that knowledge.

12Formerly, in the Dvapara age, you did not continue the Yadu line;3
now your lineage will spread in the world."

13Nityananda said: "You do everything.
You are the player, and I am like the instrument.

14Whatever you make me do, wherever you turn me,
who is so independent as to shake his head at it?

15And for me in particular you are destroyer, maker and sustainer;
you make me do both wrong and right;4 my very being is in you alone.

[p. 16]

16Making me an avadhuta, you made me wander the world,
while you, drawing a veil over my eyes, stayed hidden.

17After long days you showed yourself to me,
kept me near you and so fulfilled my life.

18With your prema you made me dance a great deal;
giving me bhakti, you made me a devotee, made me a Vaishnava.

19Decking me in splendid ornaments,5 you made me a man of the world;
I myself cannot understand what I am from one moment to the next.

20And now again you tell me to lead a worldly life,
though you yourself accepted the dharma of a renunciant (yati).

21Giving up the craving for women, I came to crave kirtan;
renouncing all enjoyments, I am a beggar indeed.

22Why do you punish me so, Gosai?
You are my only refuge; I have no other.

23You are the friend of my soul, you are my very life;
you are the lord of my life, the treasure of my heart.

24I am a servant who carries out orders, and I cannot transgress an order:
whatever you command, I bear it on my head."

25Having said this, Nityananda fell silent.
The Lord took him by the hand and began to speak:

26"You are Nityananda, bliss (ananda) embodied;
you are the treasure-house of my happiness and wealth.

27You are the energy (shakti), and I am the possessor of energy;
without the energy, the possessor of energy exists in vain.

28At no time are you and I different:
whoever you are, that am I — there is no difference at all.

29He who regards you and me as different
is a low man: he will never understand my work.

30As a lentil splits into two halves,6
so you and I are one, not different bodies.

31You and I are one body and one life;
we have descended in the Kali age to accomplish our task.

32Therefore in you alone are my happiness and my power:
now I appear, now I manifest (within the heart).

33All my going and speaking is by your will;
whatever I have anywhere is your help."

34Nityananda replied: "Your words are full of guile!
In how many ways you talk to win my trust!7

35Formerly you taught the gopis knowledge of Brahman
and sent them yoga by the hand of Uddhava.8

36They gave up everything to worship you, yet did not obtain your company:
tormenting your own people has always been your sport.

37You have left mother and father and [...] forlorn9 —
what can we, your destitute servants, say to that?

38Whatever you say, that I have to do:
who can transgress a word that cannot be transgressed?

39Tell me truly: when shall I see you again?
How shall I bear the pain of separation from you?"

[p. 17]

40The Lord said: "Do not come here every year:
by merely wishing it you will see me.

41In your dancing and in my mother's cooking10
you will find me without a doubt — in these two places.

42Soon I shall end these pastimes and disappear,
and then I shall appear again in your house.

43Not even the Vedas know my hidden incarnation;
I am telling you the secret of my heart.

44Truly, truly I say it — it will never be otherwise:
my coming will take place in your house."

45Hearing this, Nityananda fell down and rolled in the dust at his feet,
and Chaitanya came to him.

46Embracing each other, the two wept,
and so they spent that night without sleep.

47In the morning the two Lords, having performed their daily rites,
went and gazed unblinking at the beauty of Jagannatha.

48From that day, what a state came over the Lord!
Ceaselessly he spoke the language of separation from Krishna.

49Day and night, absorbed in Radha's mood,
he tasted all the pain of separation from Krishna.

50He tasted Radha's virtues with Svarupa alone;11
none but the most intimate devotees know this rasa.

51Upholding the dharma of the age, the sankirtana of Krishna's name —
in these two rasas Sri Shachinandana was immersed.12

52Tasting the rasa of feeling and the rasa of the name,
he practised it himself and so taught the people of the world.

53All the secret talks he had had with Nityananda
he revealed in their essence only to his intimate devotees.

54No one learnt this deepest secret;
only the Lord (Nityananda) understood the whole of the Lord's mind.

55By hints he told it to his intimate devotees;
apart from them, no one knows these things.

56One by one the devotees, on the pretext of pilgrimage,
took leave at the Lord's feet and departed.

57Nityananda came away through Gauda,
taking a number of mahantas with him.

58Road after road he went on in the bliss of love for Krishna,
reeling like one drunk on honey.

59Overwhelmed by the rasa of Gaura-Govinda,
he flooded all the people, bestowing the power of prema.

[p. 18]

60As before, he came to the bank of the Ganga,
to the village of Panihati, to Raghava's house.13

61Hearing of it, all the people came, mad with joy:
women, old men and children all longed to see him.

62From as far as Triveni14 to the village of Panihati
people came without pause to see the kirtan.

63How many people ate there, and how many more carried food away15 —
who brought and who gave, there was no telling.

64By day feasting and by night kirtan;
only Ananta could tell how many people came.

65At the time of the dancing, how many kirtaniyas sang,
how many waved peacock-feather fans and chamaras!

66On his head a loosely wound turban, earrings in his ears;
his face, outshining the moon, glitters.

67Armlets and bracelets on his arms, rings on his fingers;
on his neck a sapphire sways, and [...] a chain.16

68On his lotus feet golden anklets jingle:
merely by hearing them, sin and torment go far away.

69Streams pour from his lotus eyes and run down his face,
as if bees had stirred a lotus and made its honey overflow.

70Neck like a lion's, shoulders like an elephant's, a huge body;
arms reaching to the knees — a mighty wrestler-hero.

71His ruddy body quivers with prema;
ever greedy for kirtan, ever devoted to Gaura.

72"Gauranga! Gauranga!" he roars again and again;
what wondrous impulses — no one can understand them.

73Crying "Krishna! Krishna!" he leans now right, now left,
like a maddened elephant swaying under the blow of the goad.

74Rolling his eyes, he laughs from moment to moment;
"Yes, yes!" he says, speaking sweetly.

75And sometimes he stays silent with closed eyes,
seeing in his heart Shyamasundara, the best of dancers.

76On regaining outer awareness, drunk with prema, he roars
and weeps, calling out: "O Krishna! O my father!"

77"Where have you gone, lord of my life, son of Nanda?
If I do not find you, I shall give up my life.

78Alas, alas, son of Nanda, with the flute at your lips!
Where shall I go, where shall I find you? My heart is breaking!

79Come, smiling, and show yourself to me;
embrace me and keep me alive!"

80Sometimes, with joined palms, he calls out "Prabhu!";
sometimes he hides his face in his cloth.

81Again and again he weeps, saying "Lord of my life!";
he dashes his body to the ground and cannot be still.

82In the raganuga mood the Lord's mind is full of pride:
"Radha is the queen of my life; I am one of hers."17

[p. 19]

83Sometimes, in the mood of Rama, the Lord sways intoxicated,
saying only this: "Hey there! Hey there!"18

84"Come, Krishna, let us take the cows to Vrindavana!" —
so the Lord says at times in the mood of friendship (sakhya).

85"Brother! Brother!" he cries, and sometimes laughs;
he asks the Creator for wings to fly into the sky.

86Thus moods arise in Nityananda;
in what mood he does what is hard to understand.

87Who can understand Nityananda's transformations,
whose limit even Aja, Bhava and Shesha19 cannot reach?

88One day Nityananda rose at dawn
and went to Ambika-nagara,20 taking one servant with him —

89a merchant by caste, named Uddharana Datta,21
his associate and a very great soul.

90Waiting at the gate of Suryadasa Pandita,22
he sent Datta into the inner apartments.

91He went and announced the Lord's arrival;
hearing it, the Pandita came out and met him.

92He fell flat at his feet
and said with joined palms: "What good fortune has smiled on me!"

93The Lord said: "I have come to you:
I shall marry — give me your daughter."

94Though the brahmana knew the Lord's true nature, he was bewildered by maya,
and began to speak like a wretched man:

95"Prabhu, how can this be?
A householder bound by varna fears for his caste.

96Even though you are the complete Narayana,
still you have renounced varna, and I am a brahmana."

97Hearing this, Nityananda turned and went away;
all the people watched in amazement.

98The Pandita went inside, downcast,
and thought to himself: "My dream has come true!

99As I saw him in my dream last night,
so I have seen the Lord's feet in person.

100But I am a householder, and there is fear in my heart:
will Hari23 bring such a thing to pass for me?

101O Krishna, will the Creator really do this —
will Nityananda become my son-in-law?"

102Thinking this, he spoke within the house:
calling all his family, he told them everything.

103"At the end of last night I saw this dream:
a great personage, riding a chariot with a palm-tree banner;24

104his lustre bright and golden, his body huge,
his eyes reddish, like a mighty wrestler-hero.

105In a deep voice he was saying "Krishna, Krishna!";
his body, overcome with prema, swayed right and left.

106He came and halted the chariot at my door
and asked, laughing: 'Is this the Pandita's house?'

[p. 20]

107Resting the plough and the club on his shoulder,
he beckoned me with a sign of his hand.

108His topknot was decked with flowers, an earring in one ear;
he wore a blue dhoti, and anklets on his feet.

109His broad chest shone as if with the Kaustubha gem;
a forest garland adorned his neck, his lips were reddened.

110On them a sweet smile rained nectar;
framed by curls and tilaka, the lotus of his face sparkled.

111He said to me: 'I shall marry your daughter.
To this day you have not recognised me.'

112Having said this, he vanished;
my sleep broke, and I saw that it was already dawn."

113Vasu,25 who was inside the house, heard of the dream;
natural love welled up in her, and her eyes streamed with tears.

114She covered her face with the end of her cloth,
and the cloth was soaked with her tears.

115The kinsmen said: "This is a wonderful story!"
And someone said: "Dreams show things that are unreal.26

116Nityananda is Brahman, but such is his conduct,
and we are householders — how can we give our daughter?"

117The heart of Suryadasa Pandita was full of longing;
grieving within, he said: "Protect us, Krishna!"

118At that moment a wailing arose in the house:
"What has suddenly happened to Vasudha, what has happened?!"

119Everyone rushed into the house,
lifted her, carried her out and laid her at the door of the mandapa.

120She is unconscious, her body trembling, her eyes turned upward;
her whole body is cold, sweat streams ceaselessly down her face.

121Having examined her, the physicians determined that it was death.
"Rarely does anyone survive — the illness is apasmara.27

122It suddenly brings on sannipata," —
so saying, they treated her according to many shastras.

123Even so, there was no sign of improvement.
Packing up his medicines, the physician said:

124"Now attend to her highest welfare:
take her to the bank of the Ganga28 — your daughter is the eldest of the family."

125Hearing this, Suryadasa began to weep;
consoling him, Gauridasa said:

126"It seems we have all pushed the Avadhuta away;
go, clasp his feet and bring him back.

127As long as one lives, one belongs to someone;29
once one is dead, what tie remains between anyone?

128Whoever can save her, to him we shall give the daughter —
this is the promise I declare to all."

129Everyone said: "This word is binding on us all.
Let us all go together and fall at Nityananda's feet!"

130The Lord was sitting on the bank of the Ganga beneath a banyan tree;
he was saying "Krishna, Krishna", and streams of tears flowed from his eyes.

131Gauridasa with his people fell at his feet;
the Lord raised him up with a slap.

132"You have forgotten everything, foolish cowherd boy!"30 —
saying this, the Lord embraced him round the neck.

133Gauridasa Pandita wept, clasping his feet:
"You yourself hid away31 and made me forget everything!

134You have not freed me from varnashrama-dharma and caste,
yet you can do anything — such is your lordly play.

135Now please let your holy feet come to us,
and when you have seen, do what is fitting."

[p. 21]

136Having said this, he brought the Lord into the house,
to where Vasu lay at the door of the room.

137Her body was covered with a cloth, and a radiance rose above it,
like lightning flashing in a cloud.

138From her upturned lotus eyes a stream flowed like the nectar of a flower;
her hair was curly, and a moon shone upon her brow.

139The radiance of her teeth rose above [...],32
like light moving within a bimba fruit.

140The end of the tenth state33 was showing on her body —
and at that moment a breeze from the Lord's holy body touched her.

141The fragrance of his body entered her nostrils,
and, as at the touch of the mrita-sanjivani,34 she regained consciousness.

142With the cloth that covered her body she covered her face,
and crying "What is this, what is this?!" went into the house.

143The shakti of his pastimes took possession of Nityananda:
seated in the courtyard, he assumed a six-armed form.35

144In the upper hands, bow and arrows; in the middle, the holy plough and club;
in the two lower hands he held a staff and a water-pot.

145A crown shone on his head, earrings in his ears;
jewelled ornaments sparkled all over his body.

146Seeing this, all the people fell down and rolled on the ground;
the Pandita, with joined palms, offered praises.

147All the brahmanas were astonished at the sight —
and as they watched, he resumed the form of the Avadhuta.

148Laughing, he sat down on the platform of the Vishnu-mandapa;
brahmanas and Vaishnavas all cried: "Live, live!"36

149Everyone said: "The brahmana Suryadasa is fortunate:
he has gained Narayana himself as son-in-law!"

150They served him and relieved his fatigue.
"If the brahmana does not accept him now, his mind is deluded."

151All the pandits, kulins and kulacharyas37
took counsel together and came to one opinion:

152"We shall perform the Vedic rite and give him the sacred thread again,
reciting the gotra of his former ashrama, as custom requires."38

153This was announced to the Lord;
laughing loudly, the Lord agreed:

154"Do whatever you do; the responsibility is not mine:
in all this only Chaitanya Gosai is independent."

155Hearing this, everyone rejoiced,
and Pandita Gosai began to prepare all that was needed.

156The preparations were like those for a prince's wedding;
brahmanas were gathered from many lands.

157He invited all the people round about;
quantities of areca nuts and betel were brought.

158The brahmana summoned an acharya-astrologer,
who reckoned carefully and fixed an auspicious day.

159From that day there was a festival every day:
all the kinsmen and friends came and gathered.

160The musicians played all kinds of instruments;
every day hundreds upon hundreds of brahmanas were fed.

161To the women they distributed sindur, areca nuts and betel,
rice,39 sweets and much else of every kind.

162One day the brahmanas gathered together
and, half in jest, asked the Lord:

163"How is Sripada's meal prepared each day?
Do you cook yourself, or is there a brahmana?"

164The Lord said: "Sometimes I cook myself,
and when I cannot, Uddharana cooks and takes it off the fire.40

[p. 22]

165In this way, by turns, the cooking is done."
Hearing this, everyone was astonished.

166They said: "What caste is this Vaishnava?
What was his name in his former ashrama, and where does he live?"

167The Lord said: "He lives in Triveni;
seeing that he was a suvarna-banik,41 I accepted him."

168Hearing this, all the brahmanas began to laugh:
they understood that the Lord acts by his own will.

169Who has the power to say anything at all to him
who dwells eternally in the hearts of all?

170If he makes one speak, then one will speak;
otherwise, who is able to utter a word?

171He by whose power the living being speaks and moves —
who has the strength to argue with him?

172He is the independent Lord: who can understand his pastimes?
To deliver souls, the Lord plays such games.

173The next morning all the brahmanas,
having performed their sandhya and ahnika, came all at once.

174Sacrificial wood, flowers, [...],42 kusha grass and kusha seats,
mortar and pestle, the sacrificial ladle and all else that was required;

175staff, water-pot, umbrella, sandals, ghee,
the mekhala girdle, kaupina, black antelope skin and the sacred thread.

176Having performed the sacrifice and the rest according to the Vedas,
the priest said to Nityananda: "Atra agaccha!" ("Come here!")

177Nityananda sat in the circle of brahmanas;
according to the shruti, oblations of ghee blazed in the fire.

178Having done everything by the Vedic rules written in the shastras,
they placed the staff and water-pot in his hands.

179A ruddy kaupina, an outer cloth, a bag on his shoulder —
"Bhavati bhiksham dehi!" ("Lady, give alms!") he said to the mother.43

180Suryadasa's wife respectfully
brought gold and silver coins and gave them as alms.

181The priest said: "For the giving of the bride..."
Nityananda replied: "All that is in my mind."44

182Having said this, he whispered something in the priest's ear;
the priest replied: "Indeed so — why should it not be?"

183Holding the staff and water-pot, the Lord laughs loudly;
again and again, three times, he acts this out.

184With sandals on his feet and an umbrella on his shoulder he walks away —
to everyone he looks like a newly initiated boy brahmachari.

185Seeing that form, the women said, laughing:
"In our hearts we feel this must be Rama, the elder brother!"45

186The Lord entered the main house
and stayed there thus in seclusion for three days.46

187Very early in the morning, having looked upon the sun there,
he came out, and all gazed upon the brahmana's face.

188Bowing to Vishnu, on a low seat
sat the charming Nityananda-chandra.

189All the women of the town, arm in arm,
came by the hundreds to the Pandita's house.

190Their mouths full of betel, their eyes lined with kohl,
swaying their bodies, they all came now.

191The priest came to perform the adhivasa;47
the women raised the ululation on all sides.

192He went and tied the thread on the hands of both;
Vasu Devi, with bowed head, entered the house.

193Outside, much auspicious music was played;
in great joy many people came and went.

[p. 23]

194The women of the town went to perform the water rite;48
many of them said: "Vasu is fortunate!

195Who else has won so handsome a man?
It is as when Revati of old obtained her bridegroom."

196Some said: "It is like Parvati united with Shankara";
some said: "Like Kamala with Narayana."

197Some said: "It is the union of Kamadeva and Rati";49
some said: "This sight is Sita and Rama."

198Some said: "The youthful Lovers of Vrindavana";
some said: "The beauty of the two cannot be told.

199The radiance of the bridegroom's body is beyond words;
the lustre of the bride's body enchants the world."

200Some said: "Truly Lakshmi and Narayana:
as the groom, so the bride — they enchant Kandarpa himself."

201Each saying whatever was in her heart,
they laughed and laughed, leaning against one another.

202Young town women, and in a wedding house at that —
in their joy they could not keep their bodies steady, holding on to each other.

203Thus the whole day passed in joy,
and the time of dusk arrived.

204The Pandita told them to dress the bride and groom;
hearing this, everyone was greatly pleased.

205Nityananda sat on the platform of the Vishnu-mandapa;
Gauridasa came and dressed the bridegroom —

206as once in Vrindavana Subala himself
charmingly dressed the son of Rohini.50

207By providence it is the very same reality — there is no doubt:
truly he is that same Rama, and this surely that same Subala.

208Nityananda by nature enchants even Ananga,
and on top of that they placed a tilaka of sandal on his forehead.

209By nature his eyes roll, drunk with prema,
and on top of that they lined them with kohl in long strokes.

210His nose is high and straight, with a tilaka of sandal on it;
the beauty of that face sparkles like the orb of the moon.

211His broad chest was adorned with camphor51
mixed with sandal — like Shringara in person.

212He wore white garments and a bright sacred thread:
a wondrous hero, as if girdled by Ananta.

213A crown on his head and earrings in his ears;
golden ornaments sparkled all over his body.

214Women skilled in the art, sitting in private,
attentively adorned Vasudha.

Raga:52

215Taking a comb in hand, she dressed the hair,
binding it at the roots with golden thread;
making three equal strands, she wove a charming braid
and bound it in the style of a kabari knot.

216Tassels of red silk, covering the ears on both sides,53
fall down the back in rows;
the little curls above the forehead, one by one,
she made into charming braids.

217With the end of a cloth she wiped her face and, looking at it closely,
applied kunkuma to it again;
she drew curls and tilaka, and put kohl on her eyes,
adorning them with long lines.

218Painting the forehead, she placed dots in rows,
and drew a design in sandal on the chin;
placing a tilaka on the nose and looking the bride over,
she then put on her ornaments.

[p. 24]

219At the tip of her nose a large pearl with a golden bead —
how it sways above the peak of her lip!
It is as if at the tip of a sesame flower a drop of nectar hung,
about to fall onto a bimba fruit.54

220A golden necklace graces her throat and breast,
and they gave her a golden medallion besides;
wondrously adorned, it sways in the middle of her breast,
shining like the shield of Ananga.

221In her ears they put golden champa-flower earrings, like the angles of lightning,
hanging low over her shoulders;
the lightning, fickle by nature, stayed fixed in one place,
longing to touch her shoulder.

222Golden bracelets on her arms, new conch-shell bangles on her wrists,55
and beside them golden kankana bangles;
golden anklets were put on her feet with great love,
and her holy feet were reddened with lac.

223Dressing her in white garments and placing betel in her mouth,
they hung a fragrant flower garland round her neck;
they anointed her with sandal and added the divine scent of aguru,
mixing it with camphor.

224Sri Jahnava and Nityananda — the pair of lotus feet of both
holding ceaselessly in his heart,
Vrindavana Dasa sings their pastimes and virtues:
his heart is set on that.56

225All the kinsmen, gathering together, spoke to the Pandita;
everyone said the bridegroom should go in procession.

226Hearing this, the Pandita agreed:
"What everyone desires is my duty."

227Hearing this, everyone ran joyfully in all directions
to gather whatever was needed.

228They brought a splendid chaturdola palanquin57
to the Pandita's door and seated the Lord on it.

229All the musicians played in one tune;
hundreds upon hundreds of instruments rose to the sky.

230Dancers and singers sang in well-tuned melody,
in splendid garments and ornaments, in the Lord's presence.

231Nityananda went playfully through the town;
joyful, auspicious sounds arose on every side.

232Row upon row, the women of the town stood at their doors;
many ran along with babies in their arms.

233How many boys ran on ahead,
how many, mad with joy, sang hundreds of songs!

234Rockets and fireworks shot up, touching the sky;58
hundreds of thousands of lamps were lit.

235By their radiance the night looked almost like day;
hundreds of Vidyadharis went along dancing.

236All the gods came, taking human form,
and gazed their fill at the Lord's beauty.

237What joy there was among gods and men cannot be told!
Such pastimes does Prabhu Nityananda Raya perform.

238In the Kali age the Lord performs such pastimes;
these are pastimes hidden even from the Vedas, hard to understand.

239Thus, having gone round the town, Nityananda
rose at the Pandita's door like the full moon.

240The Pandita came and took him by the hand,
and, offering incense, lamp, sandal and a flower garland at his feet,

241led him with a stream of water to the place of the wedding;
all the women together raised the ululation.

242Nityananda stood upon a low wooden seat;
the radiance of his body made every quarter sparkle.

[p. 25]

243All the brahmanas, holding rows of lamps in their hands,
circled Nityananda seven times.

244All the women laughed, covering their faces with their cloths,
and leaned against one another.

245The bride was brought on a splendid seat
and carried round Nityananda.59

246Strewing betel and flowers, she looked upon him,
and natural love awoke in them both.

247Seeing the lord of her life after long separation,
Vasudha, in her wounded pride (abhimana),60 stood with bowed head.

248Then they carried her back into the house,
and all the brahmanas performed the rites according to rule.

249With many kinds of vessels, garments and ornaments
the Pandita himself performed the honouring (varana) of his son-in-law.

250Then they brought the bride and performed the giving away (sampradana),
all in due order, as the Vedas prescribe.

251The bride and groom were led into the house,
and in the bridal chamber (basara)61 a splendid bed of flowers was spread.

252All the witty young women entered the room
and stayed awake in the basara with games and jests.

253Thus in joy the night turned to dawn;
having bathed, the Lord sat down to the kushandika rite.62

254He performed all the sacrifices and rites according to the shastras,
and then hundreds upon hundreds of brahmanas were fed.

255In this way several days passed in joy.
One day Nityananda Raya, sitting in the house,

256was eating rice, Krishna's prasada,
and Sri Jahnava63 was serving him dishes again and again.

257She is Suryadasa's daughter, Vasu's younger sister;
from childhood she had been devoted to Nityananda.

258As she served, the cloth slipped from her head,
and with two more arms she modestly set her garment right.64

259Seeing this, Nityananda reflected in his mind
and knew for certain: "This is my complete shakti."

260Having rinsed his mouth (achamana), the Lord sat on the bed;
at that time Vasu-Lakshmi came to him.

261The Lord drew her to him and seated her at his left;
feeling the Lord's touch, the goddess floated in the rasa of bliss.

262With a soft, gentle smile she took betel with camphor
and joyfully placed it in the Lord's mouth.

263At that time Sri Jahnava came there too;
seeing the Lord, she was overcome with shyness.

264Seeing this, Nityananda took her hand, drew her to him
and seated Jahnava at his right.

265Knowing in his heart that she was the beloved of his life,
the Lord reflected, and the next day

266said this to Suryadasa Pandita:
"I take your younger daughter as dowry."65

267Hearing this, Pandita Gosai agreed:
"Is there anything of mine that I could not give you?

268My caste, my life, my wealth, my house and my family —
all at once I have surrendered at your feet."

[p. 26]

269Having said this, the Pandita, raising his arms,
full of prema, dances and cries: "Hari! Hari!"

270"O Krishna, O Yadava! When will you make it so
that my body, speech and mind abide in Nityananda?"

271Calling his family together, he told them all this;
"Good, good!" they said, laughing.

272"Through your connection we too have attained our life's fulfilment:
who has the power to transgress the Lord's command?"

273All of them, with joined palms, said to the Pandita:
"In the Kali age you have bought Krishna himself!"

274Thus Nityananda Raya in Ambika
immersed the people in the ocean of the bliss of prema.

275Thus Nityananda performed his pastimes at will,
always taking his pleasure with Sri Vasu and Jahnava.

276One day Nityananda, manifesting his majesty (aishvarya),
sported smilingly with his two beloveds.

277The Lord, Haladhara,66 lay on the bed of Ananta,
and his two beloveds served him on the bed.

278Vasu-Lakshmi served the Lord's feet,
while fair-faced Sri Jahnava, softly smiling,

279placed betel with camphor in the Lord's mouth;
on all sides their companions, the sakhis, surrounded them in service.

280Some waved chamaras, others fans;
how beautiful was the Lord's holy face with its gentle smile!

281His radiance, outshining millions of moons, had no end;
Ananta held over him an umbrella of a thousand hoods.

282Aja, Bhava and the others, with joined palms,
Sanaka, Narada, Vyasa and Shuka, the best of sages —

283all offered praises, crying "Prabhu! Prabhu!"
His body sparkled, glowing with masses of light.

284The great effulgence pervaded everything, outside and in.
Suryadasa and Gauridasa were inside the house;

285seeing the great effulgence, all were amazed,
and the two brothers ran to their son-in-law's chamber.

286They saw the Lord lying on the bed,
and beside the Lord the two daughters, four-armed.

287His lustre was bright, golden-white, his body lovely;
he was four-armed, in blue garments, with tinkling bells at his waist.

288His whole body was adorned with ornaments of every kind;
a forest garland hung down to his knees.

289In two hands shone the holy plough and club,
and with the other two, holding beads, he chanted Krishna's name.67

290Seeing him, all his associates, radiant with light,
cried "Prabhu! Prabhu!" and praised him without end:

291"Glory to Baladeva! Glory, glory to Sankarshana!
What a Lord, what a form — it cannot be told!"

292Seeing this, the two brothers fell senseless,
crying: "Glory, glory to Balarama!"

293Seeing this, Prabhu Nityananda withdrew his majesty
and, saying "Rise, rise!", lifted them up.

294At the Lord's touch both regained consciousness,
and the two brothers clasped the Lord's two holy feet.

295The two brothers offered praises, with cloths round their necks;
the merciful Lord smiled, looking at them both.

296"Birth after birth you two are Krishna's dear servants" —
so the Lord reassured them both.

297Taking leave, the two departed,
knowing him to be the complete, eternal Brahman.

298The Lord resolved to establish his shripat at Khardaha68
and, to carry out the Lord's command, to open a market (hat) of prema there.

[p. 27]

299Having resolved this, he went to the village of Khardaha
and manifested there the abode of his own pastimes.

300The Lord performed all the duties of a householder
and established the service of the deity Sri Shyamasundara.

301Sri Vasu and Jahnava both served his feet;
the Self-willed Lord imparted to each of them a certain shakti.

302The Lord sported with his two beloveds,
roaming in manifold happiness, in the delight of love's joy.

303Enjoying all kinds of rasa with his two beloveds,
he fulfilled the heart's desires of both.

304There was no limit to the joy of his two beloveds:
having obtained such a husband as Nityananda, they were lost in prema.

305Both prayed at the feet of Chaitanya:
"Birth after birth, may Nityananda be our husband!"

306The power of bhakti is manifest in Jahnava and Vasu69 —
this hidden pastime Vrindavana Dasa relates.

Thus ends the first chapter of Sri Nityananda Prabhu's Vamsha-vistara, in the Adi-lila, entitled "The Cause of Sri Virachandra's Descent".

✦

Translator's notes

Notes

  1. Samsara here means family life, the householder ashrama. Nityananda was an avadhuta, a wandering renunciant not bound by the rules of varnashrama.
  2. Nityananda's son Virachandra (Virabhadra) is regarded in the tradition as a reappearance of Chaitanya himself; hence the title of the chapter.
  3. The sense of the line is unclear. Nityananda is identified with Balarama; at the end of the Dvapara age the Yadu clan perished in internecine strife. Literally: "formerly, in Dvapara, you did not make the Yadu line."
  4. "Right" (sukarma) is restored from copy B ("nukanma"); the word is garbled in copy A.
  5. Parabhusha, "supreme, splendid ornaments". According to the Chaitanya-bhagavata, in Bengal Nityananda wore gold ornaments and rich clothes, which scandalised many.
  6. The copies read "mantrera" / "manthavera ḍāila"; restored from the sense as "masurera ḍāila", split lentils (dal): a single seed that falls apart into two halves.
  7. Patiyana, "trust, belief" (cf. pratyaya).
  8. An episode of the Bhagavata Purana (10.46–47): Krishna sends Uddhava to Vraja to console the gopis with teachings on knowledge and yoga.
  9. The middle of the line is corrupt in both copies ("īaidre" / "gaitdhe"). It may allude to Krishna leaving Nanda and Yashoda, or to Chaitanya leaving his mother Shachi and his wife Vishnupriya when he took sannyasa.
  10. The copies read "mātāra vandhane" ("in my mother's bonds"); corrected to "randhane" ("cooking") after the well-known motif: Chaitanya is always present in Shachi's cooking, Nityananda's dancing, Srivasa's kirtan and Raghava's house (Chaitanya-charitamrita, Antya 2).
  11. Svarupa Damodara, Chaitanya's closest companion in Puri, with whom he shared his experiences in Radha's mood.
  12. Shachinandana, "the son of Shachi", i.e. Chaitanya.
  13. Panihati is a village on the Ganga north of Calcutta. Raghava Pandita was an associate of Chaitanya, famous for the bags of delicacies (Raghavera jhali) that he sent to Puri every year.
  14. Triveni, the sacred confluence of three rivers (Ganga, Yamuna and Sarasvati) in the Hooghly district.
  15. "vāri laẏa", literally "take water"; possibly "vāṛai laẏa", "take home". The rendering is conjectural.
  16. The passage is corrupt: the copies read "*thete" / "+ṇete śikali"; where the chain is worn (at the waist?) is unclear.
  17. Raganuga, bhakti that follows the passionate love of the residents of Vraja. Here Nityananda sees himself as one of Radha's servants.
  18. Nityananda is held to be Balarama (Rama), Krishna's elder brother; "kire!" is a familiar cowherd's call.
  19. Aja (Brahma), Bhava (Shiva) and Shesha (Ananta).
  20. Ambika-nagara is Ambika Kalna on the Ganga, where the brothers Suryadasa Pandita and Gauridasa Pandita lived.
  21. Uddharana Datta Thakura, an associate of Nityananda from the suvarna-banik (gold-merchant) caste, from Saptagram.
  22. The name is restored: it is garbled in the copies ("ādhā dāsa" / "kavaṇya dāsa"), but the following text shows that Suryadasa Pandita is meant.
  23. "hari" is restored from the rhyme (kari — hari); the word is garbled in the copies.
  24. The chariot with the palm-tree banner (taladhvaja), the plough and club, the single earring and the blue garments are all emblems of Balarama.
  25. Vasu is Vasudha, Suryadasa's elder daughter.
  26. Reading "avastu", "unreal"; the copies have "vanuvastu" / "vavasthā".
  27. Apasmara, epilepsy; sannipata, in Ayurveda a dangerous derangement of all three doshas, often fatal.
  28. By custom the dying are carried to the bank of the Ganga.
  29. The line is conjecturally restored, reading "tatakṣaṇa vā kāhāra" for the corrupt "vākhāra".
  30. Nityananda-Balarama addresses Gauridasa as a cowherd of Vraja: Gauridasa is held to be Subala, the friend of Krishna and Balarama.
  31. Reading "lukāilā", "hid"; copy A has "luṭila"; in B the line is barely legible.
  32. The word "asvali" / "anthali" cannot be confidently restored (perhaps "adhara", "lips"). The bimba fruit is a conventional simile for red lips.
  33. The tenth state is the last of the ten stages of love in separation, i.e. death.
  34. Mrita-sanjivani, the miraculous herb that revives the dead.
  35. Reading "prāṅgaṇe āsīna", "seated in the courtyard". The six-armed form combines features of Rama (bow and arrows), Balarama (plough and club) and a sannyasi (staff and water-pot).
  36. "jiẏae jiẏae", "live, live!"; possibly also "she lives, she lives!" — of Vasudha.
  37. Kulins are brahmanas of the highest Bengali lineage rank; kulacharyas are genealogists who arrange marriages.
  38. As a sannyasi Nityananda had no sacred thread and belonged to no varna. To marry he had to undergo the upanayana again, with the gotra of his family before renunciation being named.
  39. "cala" / "ṭahala" — probably "cāla", "rice"; the reading is conjectural.
  40. Uddharana is not a brahmana, so the brahmanas are astonished that he cooks for a former sannyasi.
  41. The suvarna-baniks, gold merchants, were considered a low caste in Bengal at the time: brahmanas would not accept food from their hands.
  42. The word is corrupt ("jāna" / "jani").
  43. Part of the upanayana rite: the newly initiated brahmachari asks his mother (here, Suryadasa's wife) for his first alms, then, taking up his staff, acts out leaving for his studies, and is persuaded to stay and marry.
  44. The priest apparently raises the matter of giving away the bride, urging the "brahmachari" to stay; Nityananda's reply is playful.
  45. Rama is Balarama, Krishna's elder brother.
  46. Couplet 186 is missing in copy A and is taken from copy B. By custom the newly initiated spends three days in seclusion.
  47. The adhivasa is a pre-wedding rite of consecration; an auspicious thread is tied on the hands of bride and groom. The ululation (ulu-dhvani, hulahuli) is the jubilant cry of Bengali women at festivities.
  48. "jala sahivāre": a wedding rite in which the women go in procession to fetch water.
  49. The copies read "rañjita" / "raptita milana"; we read it as the union of Kamadeva with Rati.
  50. The son of Rohini is Balarama; his cowherd friend Subala is traditionally held to have appeared in Gaura-lila as Gauridasa Pandita.
  51. Ghanasara, camphor. Shringara is the erotic rasa personified.
  52. "yathā rāga", an indication of the melody; the name of the raga is not given in the edition. A tripadi follows, in four-line stanzas.
  53. "raṅgana pāṭera thopā", tassels of silk the colour of the rangan flower (red); "covering the ears" ("karṇa jhā~pā") is a conjectural interpretation.
  54. The nose is compared to a sesame flower, the lips to the red bimba fruit.
  55. Reading "kare nava śaṅkha" (a conch-shell bangle, the sign of a married woman in Bengal); the copies have "kāra nava saṅga" / "kare nava saṅga".
  56. The end of the stanza, in Brajabuli, is garbled ("tahāla dhara bhela cita"); we read it as "tahi~ lālasa bhela cita", "the heart longs for that".
  57. A chaturdola is an ornate palanquin carried by four bearers.
  58. Reading "hāui ātasa", "rockets and fireworks"; the copies are badly garbled.
  59. In the Bengali rite the bride, seated on a wooden board, is carried seven times round the groom, after which comes the shubhadrishti, the couple's first look at each other.
  60. Abhimana, the wounded pride of love. Vasudha and Jahnava are held to be Balarama's eternal consorts (Revati and Varuni); hence the "long separation".
  61. The basar-ghar, the bridal chamber, where on the first night the couple and their friends stay awake with jests and songs.
  62. The kushandika is the concluding fire rite of a Bengali wedding.
  63. Jahnava Devi, Suryadasa's younger daughter and Nityananda's second wife; after his passing she became the head of the Vaishnava community.
  64. A well-known tradition: Jahnava manifested two more arms to set right her slipping veil without stopping serving the food. "pariveśite" ("while serving") is restored from "pāgaśite" / "pāḥśite".
  65. Yautuka, a dowry or wedding gift.
  66. Haladhara, "the bearer of the plough", a name of Balarama; the bed of Ananta is the serpent Shesha, on whom the Lord reclines.
  67. Literally "holding in his hand, he chants Krishna's name", i.e. with beads.
  68. Reading "śrīpāṭa" and "hāṭa" (rhyme): the copies have "kapāṭa" / "jhvapāṭa" and "sthāṭa" / "chāṭa". A shripat is the holy seat of a Vaishnava teacher; Khardaha is a village on the Ganga north of Calcutta, later the family seat of Nityananda's descendants.
  69. The line can also be read as "bhakti is manifest in Jahnava, and shakti in Vasu".
